A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIS dataset and MIRage safety fine-tuning study. The main text, tables, figures, equations, and Appendices A–E are readable and sufficiently complete for comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, ablations, and case studies, including Tables 1–10 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds model comparisons, fine-tuning outcomes, and an experiment withholding safety categories.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the four-stage MIS construction pipeline, safety CoT labels generated by InternVL2.5-78B, and MIRage training with 4,000 safety examples plus 500 general examples. The additional backbone experiments apply this existing procedure; Appendix E changes are editorial.

E1.justification: v2 newly evaluates the Privacy and Self-Harm portions of VLSBench in Figure 5; v1 used VLSBench as a construction source and discussed it without reporting this evaluation. Existing MIS subsets and general and safety benchmark coverage otherwise remain.

E2.justification: Comparison coverage expands substantially. Table 1 adds Textual SFT and VLGuard-R for LLaVA-v1.5-13B; Table 4 adds LLaVA-OV-7B; Table 5 adds a general-data-rich VLGuard-R variant. Tables 8–9 also add Textual SFT and VLGuard-R comparisons against Qwen2-VL MIRage, beyond the base-versus-MIRage comparisons in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds a category-exclusion training/evaluation design, fine-tuning experiments on MiniCPM-V 2.6 and LLaVA-OV-7B, and a VLGuard-R control reported as using 75% general data. Existing benchmark splits and evaluators remain unchanged. The new control's exact sample count is inconsistent: Section 4.2 says 5,000 additional examples, while Tables 5 and 7 say 6,000.

E4.justification: New Figure 5 directly tests transfer after excluding Privacy and Self-Harm from MIS training, using corresponding MIS, VLSBench, and MM-SafetyBench categories. Table 5 adds a substantially larger general-data control to examine the helpfulness gap. Existing input-format controls, CoT tests, taxonomy analyses, and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results across Tables 1, 4, 5, and 8–10 and Figure 5, while retaining most matched earlier scores. New MIRage MIS-easy ASRs are 1.91% for MiniCPM-V 2.6 and 1.55% for LLaVA-OV-7B. Table 9 removes the earlier Qwen2-VL MM-SafetyBench, FigStep, and JailbreakV columns. Its new MiniCPM SIUO comparison also shows MIRage below VLGuard-R, 38.32% versus 49.70%.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2.1 retains the same ASR, RSR, HR, and RR definitions; v2 merely numbers their equations separately. No substantive assumptions, mathematical reasoning, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about a safety visual reasoning gap, MIS as the first multi-image safety dataset, and improved safety without sacrificing general performance. The headline average-accuracy improvement is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 extends its interpretation of generalization to categories omitted from MIS fine-tuning. It also interprets the larger VLGuard-R general-data control as mitigating over-prudence without resolving generalization limitations. The existing adversarial-vulnerability qualification and explanation of MSSBench scoring failures remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 and Table 7 add learning rates, epochs, and framework information for the additional models, including Swift for LLaVA-OV and LlamaFactory for MiniCPM. Existing prompts and access links remain. Reporting four GPU-hours instead of 30 minutes on eight GPUs is compatible with the earlier resource usage, rather than evidence of increased training time.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Swift infrastructure citation by Zhao et al. for its LLaVA-OV implementation. The substantive related-work discussion and positioning relative to earlier safety methods remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized paragraph rewrites, terminology and grammar corrections, prompt copyedits, and author-affiliation updates. Section 4 loses its separately numbered Setup subsection, but the overall narrative and Appendix A–E organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one, with widespread table resizing and figure relocation. Figure 1 is redesigned, Figure 4 changes from stacked to side-by-side plots, and Figure 5 is added. Several tables are expanded or restructured, while existing case studies and taxonomy plots are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The additional backbone results, fuller baseline comparisons, and direct test of transfer to withheld categories strengthen the empirical support beyond v1. These benefits outweigh the limited loss of Qwen safety results, but inconsistent sample-count descriptions for the new general-data control weaken reproducibility. The revision supports a modest overall improvement without materially changing the method or resolving uncertainty about small accuracy gains.
